notes.meaning: A man who sold a house inside a walled city had one full year to buy it back. To "redeem" means to buy back. If he did not buy it back in that year, the house belonged to the buyer for good. It did not go back to him in the Jubilee, the fiftieth year when family land was returned. City houses were built by people's own work and were often used for trade. Country land was God's direct gift to each family. The year gave a seller time to rethink a rushed sale, and it gave the buyer a home he could count on.

Houses in small villages without walls were treated like farmland. They could be bought back at any time, and they went back to the family in the Jubilee. These houses belonged with the fields. A farm is not much use without a place to store crops and keep the oxen.

The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve God. They got a special rule. They could buy back their houses at any time, and any house not bought back went back to them in the Jubilee. They had no farmland like the other tribes. Their houses in their towns were all they owned. This rule showed that God took special care of them, and it kept them settled in the places God gave them.

The pastureland around the Levites' towns could never be sold. They used it to feed their cattle and flocks. It was shared land that belonged to the whole town of Levites, not to one person. So no single Levite could sell his part. It was a lasting gift to support those who served God.

If a fellow Israelite grows poor and cannot support himself, God's people must help him. The Hebrew pictures his hand shaking, like a hand held out for help. "Help him" means to take him by the arm and lift him out of his trouble. Matthew Henry says we help the poor by pity, by serving them, and by giving what they need. Poverty does not stop someone being our brother.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the words "foreigner or stranger" in this verse may have been added later by an editor.

notes.meaning: When a poor brother borrows, you must not charge him interest. You must not sell him food for a profit, either. You must not ask back more food or goods than you lent. "Fear your God" means God sees and will judge anyone who takes advantage of the poor. Older commentators say this is about loans to people in need. They say it is not about business loans for trade or land.

God gives the reason with the same words that open the Ten Commandments. He is the Lord who brought them out of Egypt and gave them the land. They had received mercy, so they should show mercy. If God has been kind to us, we should not be hard on others.

An Israelite might grow so poor that he sold himself to another Israelite as a worker. He must not be treated as a slave. He was to be treated like a hired worker who stays for a set time. He worked until the Jubilee. His master could use his work, but did not own him like a captive taken in war.

At the Jubilee he went free, and his children went with him. He went back to his family and to the land of his fathers. The master was not allowed to keep him or his family any longer. Matthew Henry sees here a picture of how Christ sets us free from the power of sin.

The reason is that the Israelites belong to God. He bought them out of slavery in Egypt, so they must never be sold as slaves forever. In Matthew Henry's words, "God does not make his servants slaves, and therefore their brethren must not." Calvin adds that the same care should be shown among Christians, who were bought by Christ's blood.

A master must not rule harshly over a poor brother who serves him. Harsh rule means work that is too hard, too long, or without enough food. It also means bullying and insults. The worker might not be able to defend himself, but God sees, and God will take his side. Adam Clarke says this rule is meant for every people, not only Israel.

Israel was allowed to buy slaves from nearby nations and from foreigners living in the land. These slaves could be passed on to children, and the Jubilee did not free them. This followed the custom of the nations at that time. But God still did not allow cruelty toward them. Israelites, though, must never rule harshly over a brother. Matthew Henry questioned using these verses to defend the slavery of Black people in his own day. Other commentators say the law limited and softened slavery rather than praising it.

A poor Israelite might sell himself to a rich foreigner living in the land. He still kept the right to be bought back. An uncle, a cousin or another close relative could pay to free him. He could also free himself if he became able to. This kept God's people from being cut off from their family and from true worship. Matthew Henry sees the close relative who buys back as a picture of Christ, who became our relative so he could set us free.

The price to buy him back was worked out fairly. They counted the years left until the Jubilee. Then they multiplied those years by a hired worker's yearly pay. If many years were left, the price was higher. If only a few were left, it was lower. This was fair to both the owner and the worker.

While he served, he was to be treated like a worker hired year by year. The foreign owner must not treat him harshly "in your sight." That means his fellow Israelites must keep watch. If they saw him being mistreated, they were to step in and help put it right.

If no one bought him back, he and his children still went free in the Jubilee. God gives the reason again: the Israelites are his servants, whom he brought out of Egypt. They belong to God, not to any human master. Adam Clarke sees the Jubilee as a picture of what Christ does. Christ cancels our debt of sin, frees us from slavery to sin, and makes believers God's children and heirs.
